prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Not, Angels, They

outputs.L1:
Not that I understand things. Angels do not walk toward the ship in the old engraving, where the moon casts a river of light—how angels might walk upon the ocean, if they wished to walk.

They do not. They hover. There is so much space between them and what shines like waves, which cannot be a choice: not for the angels, nor for the engraver, who was, in fact, Gustave Doré, after sleeping off the ancient mariner Coleridge left behind beneath guilt and regret and the weight of an albatross.

Which is not much, perhaps, though they are large animals—four feet across, counting the wind involved, and the rain. Doré waking to a room not really of wings. I imagine a stirring, something in the black expanse he hoped to incise into the copper plate—no, with a graver, not a razor at all.

Beauty does terrify: a bare nothing, but stop. As with angels. Abrupt. Still, to cut them their flight in metal takes time. His hands stiff, Doré under a deadline, no doubt, as the small, endlessly later rest of us do what we do, and do it until it is no longer what we do.

Nevertheless, angels. Why did they keep coming, one by one: radiant, dark, out of a mind paused before this most desolate given—water at night. That it floods a future not even in the picture.
outputs.L2:
Not because I claim to grasp it.

The angels are not moving toward the vessel,  
in that old print where the moon lays down  
a bright road across the water,  
the way angels might cross the sea  
if walking were what they meant to do.

But they do not walk.  
They remain suspended.  
There is so much distance  
between their bodies and the thing  
gleaming below like surf.

That distance cannot really be called a decision,  
not for the angels,  
nor for the maker of the engraving—  
Gustave Doré, as it turns out—  
after he had slept off the Ancient Mariner  
Coleridge had stranded in him,  
with its guilt, its remorse,  
and the burden of the albatross.

A burden not so large, perhaps,  
though albatrosses are sizable birds,  
four feet wide if you include  
the weather they carry with them,  
the wind and the rain.

Doré wakes in a room  
that is not exactly full of wings.  
Maybe only a tremor,  
some motion inside the dark vastness  
he hoped to cut into copper—  
not with a razor, no,  
with a burin, a graver.

Beauty is frightening, yes:  
a stripped-down emptiness  
that suddenly commands stillness.  
Like angels.  
Sudden. Motionless.

Even so, carving flight into metal  
is slow work.  
His fingers rigid,  
Doré surely pressed by a deadline,  
as we all are, in our small later lives,  
doing what we do over and over  
until it no longer resembles what we do.

And still: angels.

Why did they continue arriving,  
one after another,  
darkly luminous,  
out of a mind arrested  
before this bleakest fact offered to it:  
night water.

And that water, though the image does not show it,  
spills forward into a future.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on Gustave Doré’s engraving of angels suspended above a moonlit ocean, noting that they do not simply move toward a ship in a clear or comforting way. Instead, they hover in the darkness, poised between motion and stillness, presence and distance. Their placement above the water gives the scene an atmosphere of mystery rather than reassurance. The ocean below them is vast and desolate, illuminated only by moonlight, and the angels appear less like guides than like strange figures whose purpose cannot be fully understood.

The poem connects Doré’s image to Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” drawing on the poem’s themes of guilt, regret, and spiritual punishment. The reference to the albatross recalls the burden carried by the Mariner after his destructive act, a symbol of sin and consequence. In this context, the angels seem to belong not only to a religious or visionary world, but also to a world shaped by remorse. Their presence above the sea evokes the Mariner’s haunted journey, where natural beauty and supernatural terror are inseparable.

The speaker also considers the physical labor involved in making Doré’s engraving. Rather than treating the image as effortless inspiration, the poem emphasizes the slow and difficult process by which it was created. Flight, light, and beauty had to be cut into metal through repeated, careful movements of the hand. The angels’ apparent weightlessness is therefore the result of intense material effort. What looks airy and divine in the finished image was produced through pressure, resistance, and painstaking craft.

Through this attention to both subject and process, the poem suggests that beauty is not always gentle or easily understood. It can arrive suddenly, even violently, and it may inspire fear as much as wonder. The angels are beautiful, but their beauty is unsettling because it appears in a scene of darkness, isolation, and possible judgment. The poem refuses to make them simple symbols of hope. Instead, it presents beauty as something difficult: abrupt, mysterious, and capable of disturbing the viewer.

As the angels recur in the speaker’s imagination, they become a haunting presence against the bleak image of water at night. They remain suspended above the moonlit ocean, neither fully explained nor resolved. Their mystery gives the scene a sense of continuation, as though something lies beyond the boundaries of the engraving itself. The poem hints at a future beyond the picture—a movement, revelation, or consequence that has not yet arrived. In this way, Doré’s angels become more than figures in an illustration; they become signs of an unknown possibility hovering over darkness.
outputs.L4:
Gustave Doré’s engraving of angels above the ocean in Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* invites a long and unsettled gaze. At first, the image seems to offer a moment of supernatural consolation: luminous beings hover over a vast, dark sea, their forms gathered in a fragile brightness against the surrounding night. Yet the longer one looks, the less simple that consolation becomes. The angels do not abolish the darkness beneath them. They do not still the waters, explain the Mariner’s guilt, or release the world from dread. Instead, they appear suspended within the very mystery they illuminate.

Doré’s art depends on this tension between revelation and obscurity. His engraving is not merely an illustration of Coleridge’s poem; it is a meditation on the poem’s deepest atmosphere. The ocean is not simply a setting but a spiritual condition: immense, unknowable, and morally charged. Its blackness suggests loneliness, punishment, and the terrifying scale of creation. Against that darkness, the angels shine, but their radiance is not gentle in any ordinary sense. It is severe, almost frightening. Their beauty does not comfort so much as intensify the scene’s strangeness.

The image therefore becomes an ekphrastic space, a place where looking turns into thinking. One begins by noticing the details: the pale bodies, the wings, the upward movement, the emptiness of the horizon, the heavy expanse of water below. But these details soon lead beyond themselves. The engraving asks what it means to make beauty out of terror, and what kind of labor is required to render mystery visible without destroying it. Doré’s lines are precise, disciplined, and deliberate, yet they describe forces that cannot be fully mastered: guilt, judgment, grace, death, and the vast indifference of the sea.

In Coleridge’s poem, the Ancient Mariner is marked by an inexplicable crime and an equally mysterious redemption. He kills the albatross, suffers punishment, witnesses the uncanny movements of life and death, and is compelled afterward to repeat his story. Doré’s angels belong to that world of compulsion and wonder. They seem to descend from heaven, but they also seem to arise from the Mariner’s haunted imagination. Are they messengers of mercy, signs of divine order, or terrifying reminders that the human soul is never hidden from judgment? The engraving refuses to answer decisively.

This uncertainty is central to its power. The angels hover, and hovering is itself an ambiguous action. They neither arrive nor depart. They are present, but not fully accessible. Their suspended forms suggest a future that has not yet been disclosed. Something is coming—judgment, rescue, revelation, or further suffering—but the image holds that future at a distance. In this way, Doré preserves the poem’s spiritual unease. He does not translate the supernatural into something familiar. He allows it to remain overwhelming.

The beauty of the engraving lies not in resolving darkness but in placing radiance beside it. The angels are beautiful because they appear where beauty seems impossible: above desolate night water, in a world emptied of ordinary human comfort. Their light does not erase the sea’s terror; it gives that terror shape. The darkness, in turn, makes the angels more vivid, more precarious, and more strange. Doré understands that beauty is often inseparable from fear, especially in works concerned with guilt and redemption. To see the angels is not to be reassured that all is well. It is to feel that the visible world has opened onto something immeasurably larger than itself.

The engraving also reflects on artistic labor. Every line in Doré’s image is an act of pressure against blankness, a way of drawing form out of darkness. Engraving itself is a medium of incision, contrast, and patience. Light is created through cuts, through the disciplined handling of black and white. This material process echoes the moral and spiritual drama of the poem. Just as the Mariner’s story emerges from suffering, Doré’s vision emerges from darkness worked by hand. Art here is not effortless inspiration; it is a struggle with shadow.

Yet the artist’s labor does not produce certainty. Doré gives us an image of angels, but not an explanation of them. He renders the supernatural with extraordinary force while leaving its meaning open. That openness is part of the engraving’s truth. Both Coleridge and Doré understand that mystery cannot be reduced without being diminished. The Mariner’s experience exceeds doctrine, psychology, and narrative closure. It must be told again and again because it cannot be exhausted. Likewise, Doré’s image asks to be revisited because it does not settle into a single interpretation.

The angels above the ocean therefore embody a double power. They are radiant, but they are also terrifying. They suggest mercy, but they also recall judgment. They appear as figures of transcendence, yet they are bound to the darkness that surrounds them. Their presence transforms the sea into a threshold between worlds: life and death, guilt and absolution, sight and blindness, the known and the unknowable.

In the end, Doré’s engraving does what great art often does. It preserves mystery while making it felt. It gestures toward an unseen future without claiming to possess it. The hovering angels do not solve the Mariner’s suffering, nor do they dispel the night. Instead, they illuminate the depth of that suffering and the vastness of the night around it. They remind us that beauty may appear not as escape from darkness, but as a radiance trembling within it.
outputs.L5:
**Not Angels, They**

Not angels, they arrived without wings, without halos, without songs from the sky. They came quietly, wearing tired faces and ordinary shoes, carrying groceries, tools, books, and small acts of courage in their hands.

They were not perfect. They made mistakes, lost patience, forgot promises, and sometimes did not know the right words to say. But still, they stayed. They listened when silence became too heavy. They helped when no one was watching. They stood beside others in moments when kindness mattered more than perfection.

Not angels, they were people—neighbors, friends, strangers, family. Their goodness did not shine like light from heaven; it appeared in simple ways: a warm meal, a gentle message, a hand held in grief, a door opened, a burden shared.

And perhaps that is what made them beautiful. They were not angels. They were human. And still, they chose to care.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse ekphrastic poem responding to Gustave Doré’s engraving of angels hovering over the ship in Coleridge’s “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” with a fragmented, meditative voice.
counterfactuals.output:
Above the ship,  
the angels do not arrive  
so much as gather—

white pressure in the dark,  
a grammar of wings  
the sea cannot read.

Doré has made the night  
engraved,  
not black but bitten into:  
line after line  
of weather,  
of judgment,  
of the old story  
cut deep enough to shine.

The ship is small beneath them.  
All ships are small  
beneath what watches.

Masts like ribs.  
Sails like torn lungs.  
The water, a field  
of restless metal.

And there—  
the mariner, perhaps,  
or only the idea of him:  
a body sentenced  
to remember.

I keep looking  
at the hovering.

Not flying.  
Not landing.  
Held  
in that impossible pause  
between mercy  
and evidence.

Their faces are lamps  
turned inward.  
Their robes spill light  
the way wounds spill truth  
when no one asks.

What is forgiveness  
if it must be witnessed  
from above?

What is a soul  
but a ship  
with weather inside it?

The angels lean  
over the deck’s ruin,  
over the dead men  
standing again  
with borrowed motion,  
over the ancient guilt  
that will not drown.

Maybe holiness is not comfort.  
Maybe it is attention—  
unblinking,  
terrible,  
tender only after  
it has seen everything.

The engraving says:  
even the dark  
has been worked on  
by hand.

Even the curse  
has texture.

Even the sea,  
which wanted only to swallow,  
must hold the reflection  
of these pale messengers  
who come without speech,  
without rescue exactly,  
but with presence—

that other kind of weather.

I think of the albatross,  
its white weight  
at the throat.

I think of every harm  
we carry  
until it learns our name.

Above the ship,  
the angels hover,  
and the world below them  
does not heal.

Not yet.

But something has changed  
in the atmosphere:  
a loosening,  
a breath  
where there had been only salt  
and sentence.

The mariner will live  
to tell it badly,  
then tell it again.

The sea will go on  
folding and unfolding  
its dark pages.

And the angels—  
etched in their bright hesitation—  
remain suspended  
over the wreck of consequence,

not absolving,  
not accusing,

only bearing  
the unbearable light  
downward.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of a modern lyric essay-poem about an old engraving: angels above moonlit water, the Ancient Mariner, guilt, an albatross, and the labor of engraving on metal.
counterfactuals.output:
**Burin**

In the old engraving the moon is not light but pressure:  
a white coin pressed into black water,  
the sea accepting it in broken payments.

Above, angels hover like thoughts no one admits to having.  
They are made of line—  
feather by feather, wound by wound—  
their faces nicked into brightness.

Below them, the mariner stands in his borrowed weather,  
his beard a storm of little cuts,  
his eyes two harbors where no ship forgives him.

The albatross is there, or not there.  
That is the trick of guilt:  
it can hang from the neck  
even after the rope has been drawn away.

I think of the engraver bent over copper,  
lamp smoking beside him,  
hand moving slowly enough to make darkness obey.  
Not drawing, exactly. Removing.  
Not singing, exactly. Scoring silence  
until an image rises from injury.

Each wave is a decision.  
Each cloud, a hesitation.  
Each angel, a labor of the wrist.

Metal remembers differently than paper.  
It keeps the force of the tool,  
the angle of the doubt,  
the place where the hand slipped  
and made a deeper night.

So the mariner’s guilt is not moral only.  
It is material.  
A groove cut too far to burnish out.  
A bird-shaped absence inked again and again  
and pressed, damp sheet after damp sheet,  
into the world.

Moonlit water, crosshatched and restless.  
Angels above it, merciful as architecture.  
A man below, learning the long alphabet  
of consequence.

And somewhere outside the frame,  
the dead bird keeps opening its wings—  
not to fly,  
but to measure the weight  
of what a single hand can do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, enjambed free verse poem that begins “Not that I understand things” and reflects on angels, Gustave Doré, Coleridge, the ocean at night, and the terror of beauty.
counterfactuals.output:
Not that I understand things, only that sometimes  
the dark unrolls its plated wings above the water  
and every wave is a thought refusing to finish,  
black-backed, moon-cut, dragging its silver  
like a chain through the throat of the world.  

I have seen angels in Gustave Doré,  
not gentle, not the porcelain rumor of mercy,  
but engines of radiance, musculature of command,  
eyes emptied of pity by too much heaven,  
their feathers sharpened into weather,  
their hands extended as if blessing were another form  
of falling.  

Coleridge knew the mind could rot  
on a becalmed sea, that albatross of wonder  
hung from the neck until the miracle stank,  
until the beautiful became unbearable  
because it would not explain itself.  
O glittering water, O night with its innumerable  
cold mouths, I have leaned over your edge  
and felt the stars looking back like verdicts.  

There is a terror in beauty  
because it asks nothing of us  
and still takes everything—  
the breath, the name, the little lantern  
we carry through our manageable grief.  
An angel passes over the ocean  
and the ocean darkens, not from shadow  
but from recognition; the waves kneel  
and rise, kneel and rise,  
endlessly forgiven, endlessly afraid.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ekphrastic prose poem about Doré waking from dreams of Coleridge’s Ancient Mariner and trying to carve angels into a copper plate, mixing art history, doubt, and existential reflection.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn Doré wakes with salt in his beard that is not there, with the albatross still beating its judicial wings against the shutters. Paris has not yet become Paris; it is only a gray pressure behind the curtains, a city held underwater. On the table: the copper plate, reddish as a wound that has learned to shine. Beside it: burins, a candle stub, a glass clouded by last night’s wine, and the open book where Coleridge’s sea goes on happening without permission.

He has dreamed the mariner again—those eyes bright with the fever of testimony, that old mouth condemned to open and open, pouring out shipwreck, thirst, blessing, guilt. Doré sits up as if summoned to a trial. He has illustrated Hell; he has given Dante cliffs, demons, the pale musculature of the damned. He has furnished Milton with ruinous heavens and Satan with a tragic altitude. He has made the Bible flare like a storm lantern. But this—this ancient sailor with his private apocalypse—will not stay fixed.

How do you engrave a curse?

The copper waits. It has the patience of matter, which is to say the cruelty. Doré leans over it and begins to carve angels.

Not the plump ambassadors of ceilings, not Raphael’s soft putti leaning on the sill of eternity, not the gold-leaf messengers who enter Annunciations as if history were a room they could cross without staining their feet. These angels arrive from the mariner’s sky: starved, elongated, their robes shredded into weather, their faces turned aside as though even mercy has its limit. He cuts one wing, then doubts it. The line is too certain. Angels, if they exist, must be made of hesitation.

He scrapes it out.

Copper remembers every injury. Even correction leaves a ghost.

The burin bites again. A shoulder appears. A throat. A hand lifted either in blessing or refusal. Doré cannot decide which, and the ambiguity troubles him more than failure. In the dream, the sea was full of eyes. The dead sailors stood around the mast with mouths closed, and from their bodies rose something like prayer, though prayer to whom he could not tell. Above them, the angels were not rescuers but witnesses, as engravings themselves are witnesses: black lines confessing the pressure of a hand.

He thinks of all the artists who have tried to make the invisible visible and found, at the end, only style. Giotto gave grief weight and blue walls. Michelangelo gave the divine a torso, a terrible finger. Blake drew flame as if he had seen it from within. Goya looked too long at the night of reason and learned that monsters are not metaphors. And Doré—what has Doré done? He has built architectures for other men’s visions. He has stood at the threshold of their catastrophes, holding a lamp.

The plate glows under the weak morning light. It seems less like an object than a verdict.

If he carves the angel too beautifully, he lies. If he carves it hideously, he lies differently. The mariner’s tale is not about punishment alone, nor redemption alone, but about the unbearable fact of being conscious in a world that answers with weather. A bird falls. A wind stops. A soul discovers itself by the weight of what it has killed. And afterward—this is the true horror—there is still language. There is still the need to tell.

Doré lowers his head until his breath fogs the copper. For a moment he sees himself there, distorted: not the famous illustrator, not the prodigy with publishers at his door, not the maker of spectacles, cathedrals, precipices, apocalyptic crowds—but a man bent over metal, scratching darkness into light. Each line removes nothing and yet changes everything. Each incision is a wager against oblivion.

Outside, carts begin to clatter over stone. Somewhere a church bell rehearses eternity in practical intervals. Doré listens and thinks: perhaps angels are only the names we give to the distance between guilt and forgiveness. Perhaps they are the forms taken by our longing when it cannot bear to remain abstract. Perhaps they are not above us at all, but trapped in the plate, waiting for the knife to wound them into appearance.

He carves again.

Now the angel leans over the becalmed ship, and its wing is also a wave, and the wave is also a shroud, and the shroud is also the page of a book. Beneath it the mariner stares outward, not at God, not at the dead, but at the viewer—as if to say: you, too, have survived something you do not understand. You, too, have mistaken beauty for permission. You, too, have woken from dreams with your hands empty and gone looking for a tool sharp enough to make meaning.

Doré pauses. The room is fully morning. The angel on the copper is imperfect, uncertain, almost erased by its own radiance. Good, he thinks—or hopes he thinks. Doubt has entered the line. The divine, if it comes, will have to pass through doubt’s narrow gate.

He lifts the plate and turns it toward the window. In the raw copper, the angel darkens. In the darkening, it begins to live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary poem with long broken sentences and sudden corrections, centered on angels who hover instead of walk, a moonlit ship engraving, and the idea that water at night contains the future.
counterfactuals.output:
The angels do not walk anymore—  
or maybe they never did, maybe that was only our way  
of giving them knees, dust, a road,  

but tonight they hover  
three inches above the pier,  
their hems refusing the puddles,  
their faces lit from underneath  
by the black, tidal mirror of the harbor.  

One of them is holding a moonlit ship engraving,  
no—  
not holding, exactly,  
pinning it against the air with two pale fingers,  
as if the paper were a wing that wanted to leave,  
as if the ship, carved in silver lines,  
had already sailed through the hand that made it  
and entered some colder sea.  

Look at it:  
the mast thin as a vein,  
the sails swollen with a wind that died  
two centuries ago,  
the moon scratched above it  
like an unfinished thought.  

And beneath the pier the water keeps moving  
with its dark mouth closed,  
as if it knows,  
as if night is the only time water is allowed  
to contain the future—  

not reflect it, no,  
not predict,  
but contain:  

your old age folded into a wave,  
a city not yet burned trembling in the tide,  
the name of the child you will not have  
turning once beneath the pilings,  
bright and unreadable as a fish.  

The angels lean closer without bending.  
They have no need of balance.  
Their shadows hover too—  
that is the worst part,  
or the most beautiful,  
I keep changing my mind.  

One says the ship is leaving.  
One says it has arrived.  
One says nothing,  
which is how I understand  
that both are true.  

Above us, the moon loosens its white nail  
from the sky,  
and the engraved ship shivers  
as though the paper remembers being a tree,  
as though the tree remembers rain,  
as though rain remembers the ocean  
before it became anything  
so easily named.  

I want to ask the angels  
what happens next,  
but the water is already answering  
in its broken language,  

hush and drag,  
hush and drag,  

bringing forward the shape of tomorrow  
then taking it back,  
correcting itself endlessly  
in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
